<strong>Comparar bases.</strong> Fotón 1: Comparing bases. Photon 1: + and + agree. Photon 2: × and + do not. Photon 3: × and × agree. Photon 4: + and × do not. Photons 1 and 3 survive.
<strong>Eva sin errores.</strong> En cad: Eve with no errors. In each sifted bit, Eve produces an error with probability $1/4$, so she does not produce one with probability $3/4$. For four bits with no error at all: $(3/4)^4 = 81/256 \approx 0{.}32$.
<strong>La clave.</strong> En los que co: The key. In the ones that agree, Bob reads Alice's bit: photon 1 gives 1, photon 3 gives 1. Sifted key: 11. The other two Bob measured in the wrong basis and his bit is random: they are thrown away.
<strong>Lo que enseña.</strong> Con solo: What it teaches. With only four bits compared, Eve would get away 32 % of the time. That is why hundreds are compared: $(3/4)^{100}$ is practically zero, and the spy has no way out.
Ahora Eva, en medio del canal. No puede: Now Eve, in the middle of the channel. She cannot copy the photons (no cloning), so her only option is to measure them and resend them. But she does not know Alice's basis: she chooses at random, and half the time she gets it wrong. When she gets it wrong, she obtains a random bit and alters the photon. That altered photon, if Bob measures it in the right basis, now gives the correct bit only half the time. Result: in the sifted photons, Alice and Bob no longer always agree.
Alicia envía bits con bases al azar; Ben: Alice sends bits with random bases; Bob measures with random bases. The photons in which the bases agree are marked: in those the bits are equal and form the key. In the rest, Bob's bit is random and is thrown away.
Alicia envía cada bit en un fotón polari: Alice sends each bit in a polarised photon, and chooses at random one of two bases. In the rectilinear basis, the bit 0 is a vertical photon and the 1 a horizontal one. In the diagonal basis, the 0 is at 45° and the 1 at 135°. The physical rule: if a photon is measured in the same basis it was sent in, the correct bit comes out; if it is measured in the other basis, 0 or 1 at random comes out, and the photon is left changed into the basis it was measured with.
Alicia envía los bits 1,0,1,1 con bases: Alice sends the bits 1, 0, 1, 1 with bases +,×,×,+ (rectilinear, diagonal, diagonal, rectilinear). Bob measures with bases +,+,×,×. BB84 no es teoría: hay redes comerciales: BB84 is not theory: there are commercial quantum key distribution networks between banks and data centres, and fibre links of tens of kilometres. In 2017, the Chinese satellite Micius distributed quantum keys between two stations 1200 km apart, and an encrypted Beijing-Vienna video call was made with them. Its limits are practical: it needs fibre or line of sight, it does not cross the internet, and it protects the key's distribution, not the message, which is then encrypted with AES. That is why, for almost everything, the answer to the quantum computer is the post-quantum cryptography of the previous topic, which works over the network that already exists.

Diffie-Hellman reparte una clave con mat: Diffie-Hellman distributes a key with mathematics a quantum computer would break. BB84 distributes it with photons, and its security lies in no hard problem, but in a law of physics: measuring a quantum system alters it. If Eve looks at the photons to copy them, she changes them, and Alice and Bob detect it by comparing part of the key. Eve does not have to be weak; physics has to be the way it is.
El mismo protocolo, ahora con Eva midien: The same protocol, now with Eve measuring and resending each photon with a random basis. Over the sifted key, the fraction of bits that differ between Alice and Bob is counted. Switch Eve on and off and compare: without her, 0 %; with her, close to 25 %.
El protocolo, sin espía: Alicia manda mu: The protocol, with no spy: Alice sends many bits, each with a random basis. Bob, who does not know which basis Alice used, also chooses at random to measure each one. Then, over a public channel, they tell each other the bases (not the bits) and keep only the photons in which the bases agreed: half of them, on average. In those, their bits are equal. That is the sifted key.

Stephen Wiesner tuvo la idea del «dinero: Stephen Wiesner had the idea of unforgeable “quantum money” around 1970, and it was not published. Charles Bennett and Gilles Brassard turned it into a key distribution protocol in 1984, hence the name BB84, at a conference in Bangalore; the paper went unnoticed for years. In 1991 Artur Ekert gave a version based on entanglement. The first demonstration, in 1989, covered 32 centimetres of air over a table; today it is thousands of kilometres by satellite.
